\chapter{The Rest of You}
\label{ch:ta-the-rest-of-you}
\hlchaptermodality{55}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my neck, my back, a lip, a nail and a bone in Tamil.}

Complete TA-C55-bone and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kaḻuttu]{\ta{கழுத்து} (kaḻuttu) — the neck}

\label{lesson:TA-C55-neck}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{kiṇṇam} mean, and what did \emph{peṭṭi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{கழுத்து}}
\textbf{\ta{கழுத்து}} (\emph{kaḻuttu}) — \textquotedblleft{}the neck\textquotedblright{}.

Malayalam \ml{കഴുത്ത്} (\emph{kaḻuttŭ}) is the same word, \ta{ழ} and all — that letter again, the one only these two sisters still write. Telugu went its own way here, to \te{మెడ} (\emph{meḍa}).

It is the neck outside and the throat inside, both in one word. A garland goes round the \ta{கழுத்து}, and so does the thread tied at a wedding.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five more pieces of you.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kaḻuttu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{peṭṭi}, then \emph{kaḻuttu}, and hold the \ta{ழ} in the middle
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{கழுத்து} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the neck\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mutuku]{\ta{முதுகு} (mutuku) — the back}

\label{lesson:TA-C55-back}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kaḻuttu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{முதுகு}}
\textbf{\ta{முதுகு}} (\emph{mutuku}) — \textquotedblleft{}the back\textquotedblright{}.

Malayalam has \ml{മുതുക്} (\emph{mutukŭ}), letter for letter until the last one. Telugu takes \te{వీపు} (\emph{vīpu}) and shares nothing with either.

To show somebody your \ta{முதுகு} is to turn away from them, in Tamil much as in English — and the phrase is meant as unkindly in one language as in the other.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: what a garland goes round, and what you turn on somebody.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mutuku}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kaḻuttu}, then \emph{mutuku}, the top of you and the length below it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{முதுகு} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the back\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[utaṭu]{\ta{உதடு} (utaṭu) — a lip}

\label{lesson:TA-C55-lip}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mutuku} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{உதடு}}
\textbf{\ta{உதடு}} (\emph{utaṭu}) — \textquotedblleft{}a lip\textquotedblright{}.

This is where the family stops agreeing. Malayalam says \ml{ചുണ്ട്} (\emph{cuṇṭŭ}), Telugu \te{పెదవి} (\emph{pedavi}), Tamil \ta{உதடு} — three words with nothing in common but the thing they name. It happens: a part of the body every language has a name for is not therefore a part every language named at the same time.

The \ta{ட} in the middle is the one made with the tongue curled back. Keep it curled and the word comes out right.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and this one the three sisters worked out separately.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{utaṭu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{mutuku}, then \emph{utaṭu}, and curl the tongue back for the \ta{ட}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{உதடு} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a lip\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nakam]{\ta{நகம்} (nakam) — a nail}

\label{lesson:TA-C55-nail}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{utaṭu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{நகம்}}
\textbf{\ta{நகம்}} (\emph{nakam}) — \textquotedblleft{}a nail\textquotedblright{}.

The nail on a finger and the claw on an animal, in one word. Malayalam writes \ml{നഖം} (\emph{nakhaṁ}), with a breathed letter in the middle that Tamil's own set does not carry, so Tamil prints it plain: \ta{நகம்}. The two words are heard as one and written as two.

Telugu holds on to something else entirely, \te{గోరు} (\emph{gōru}).

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four: neck, back, lip, and the hard thing on the end of a finger.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nakam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{utaṭu}, then \emph{nakam}, the softest part of you and the hardest
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{நகம்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a nail\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[elumbu]{\ta{எலும்பு} (elumbu) — a bone}

\label{lesson:TA-C55-bone}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nakam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{எலும்பு}}
\textbf{\ta{எலும்பு}} (\emph{elumbu}) — \textquotedblleft{}a bone\textquotedblright{}.

Malayalam \ml{എല്ല്} (\emph{ellŭ}) and Telugu \te{ఎముక} (\emph{emuka}) sit either side of Tamil's \ta{எலும்பு}: the same opening, and then three different amounts of word after it.

\emph{elumbum tōlum} — \textquotedblleft{}bone and skin\textquotedblright{} — is what Tamil says of somebody who has gone very thin. English says the same two things in the other order.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five more of you: neck, back, lip, nail, and what holds the whole lot up.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{elumbu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{kaḻuttu}, \emph{mutuku}, \emph{utaṭu}, \emph{nakam}, \emph{elumbu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{எலும்பு} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a bone\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
